cards.title: Name the group, not the class: hydroxyl, carbonyl, amido or amino

walkthrough.question: Phenol red, bromocresol green and phenolphthalein are acid-base indicators. The drawn structures each have three benzene rings, and each shows O-H bonded to a ring. Apart from phenyl, state a functional group all three share.
walkthrough.key_idea: O-H is named hydroxyl, whatever class the molecule belongs to.
walkthrough.question_type: Name the functional group in a structure
walkthrough.careful: Give the group name, not the compound class.
procedure: Find the atoms that make up the group.
Check what is bonded next to it.
Use the syllabus group name, not the class.
Write the name unless a formula is requested.
tricks: Class to group: alcohol becomes hydroxyl; aldehyde or ketone becomes carbonyl.
N next to C=O is amido; otherwise amino. Always check the neighbour.
if_lost: Which small group of atoms appears in all three drawings?
Is the answer asking for a compound class or a group?
What is the syllabus name for this group?

1_context.short: Name a shared group across three large, unfamiliar molecules.
1_context.why: The molecules are large, but only one short syllabus name is tested. Size is a distraction.
1_context.avoid: Being put off by the sulfur and bromine atoms in the drawings.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.2: identify functional groups by name and structure, including hydroxyl and phenyl.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books label simple alcohols. This test finds the group on a ring in a large molecule and rejects the class word.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Hydroxyl or hydroxy scores; alcohol, phenol and hydroxide do not.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The mark rewards the group name. Alcohol and phenol name compound classes, and hydroxide names an ion.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Writing alcohols, the most common mistake reported in 25M.2.HL.6221.1.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Alcohol, phenol and hydroxide score zero.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: One word decides the mark: hydroxyl scores; alcohol, describing the same O-H, does not.

3_novel_application.short: Big indicators hide a one-word functional group answer.
3_novel_application.why: Functional groups are local, so the rest of the molecule does not change the group's name.
3_novel_application.avoid: Looking for an unusual group because the molecules look unusual.
3_novel_application.disguise: Three large dye structures with sulfur, bromine and several rings.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ignore the size; ask which atoms repeat in all three.

4_command_terms.short: State: one name, with no explanation.
4_command_terms.why: State asks for a specific name without explanation, so reasoning earns nothing extra.
4_command_terms.avoid: Adding a second group that could contradict the first.
4_command_terms.demands: The name of one shared group.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing, for an accepted name.

5_time_efficiency.short: Spot the repeat, write one word.
5_time_efficiency.why: This is a one-mark naming task, so the only worthwhile check is the word itself.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Comparing every part of all three molecules.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip the sulfur groups and bromines; they are not shared by all three.

6_data_booklet.short: Group names are not in the booklet sections provided.
6_data_booklet.why: Sections 20 to 22 give spectral data by bond or proton type, not a naming list for this question.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Searching the IR table for a name it was not built to give.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Halogeno, hydroxyl, carbonyl, carboxyl, alkoxy, amino, amido, ester and phenyl are NOT in the sections provided; memorise each name and structure.

7_elimination.short: Class names and ions cannot earn this mark.
7_elimination.why: The question asks for a group, so a class word or ion name fails before chemistry is checked.
7_elimination.avoid: Choosing carbonyl or carboxyl, seen in a few scripts, without checking all three structures.

definitely_wrong.rule: These name compound classes, not functional groups.
Hydroxide is an ion; this O-H is covalently bonded.
The question excludes it.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.2 functional groups by name and structure.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach class and group together; markschemes separate them and reject the class word.

trap_boundaries: Alcohol, phenol and hydroxide rejected for hydroxyl (25M.2.HL.6221.1).
Aldehyde rejected for carbonyl (25M.2.HL.6209.8).
Tertiary amino or amine accepted for a nitrogen with no adjacent C=O (25M.2.HL.6215.4).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: The structure may be read correctly and still score zero if the answer gives a class instead of the group.

disguises: -NH- inside -CO-NH-, which looks like a secondary amine.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Read the atoms next to the group before naming it.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Usually one mark per correct name, with no credit for class words.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not analyse parts of the molecule that the question does not ask about.

6_data_booklet.hack: No naming table appears in the sections provided; memorise the syllabus group list.

rules: A class name is wrong when the question asks for a functional group.
Secondary amino is wrong for -NH- directly bonded to C=O; that is amido.

evidence.note: Hydroxyl or hydroxy accepted; alcohol, phenol and hydroxide rejected.
About half correct; alcohols was the commonest error.
Carbonyl is credited; aldehyde is not accepted.
A majority gave aldehyde instead of carbonyl.
Many read -NH- in the amide linkage as secondary amine.
27% correct; most missed amido and chose secondary amino.
Students wrote amide when the nitrogen was in an amine.
Tertiary amino or amine is accepted for the nitrogen asked about.
Class names such as ketone were given in place of carbonyl.

cards.difficulty_signal: About 50% on this part in May 2025; a related SL item fell to 27% correct, with amido misread as secondary amino.

cards.title: Draw enantiomers: find the centre, then reflect in wedge-dash

walkthrough.question: Substance X, CH3CHBrC(CH3)3, has a chiral centre. Draw its two optical isomers so that the 3D arrangement around that centre is clear.
walkthrough.key_idea: Mirror one wedge-dash tetrahedron around the carbon with four different groups.
walkthrough.question_type: Draw enantiomers with wedge and dash
walkthrough.careful: Reflect only; do not also swap two groups.
procedure: Find the carbon with four different groups.
List the four groups around it.
Draw two plain bonds, one wedge and one dash.
Draw a mirror line beside the structure.
Reflect every group across that line.
tricks: Swap any two groups once for the enantiomer; swap twice returns the original.
Keep a tetrahedral shape; a flat cross with 90° angles is not accepted.
if_lost: Which carbon could have four different groups?
What four groups does that carbon carry?
What do wedge and dash bonds show?
What would the structure look like in a mirror?

1_context.short: Turn an inline formula into two 3D mirror-image structures.
1_context.why: The syllabus requires drawn tetrahedral stereochemical formulas for chiral carbons, so a flat structural formula does not meet the skill.
1_context.avoid: Drawing the structural formula twice with no 3D information.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.7: draw stereochemical formulas showing the tetrahedral arrangement around a chiral carbon.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show a ready-drawn pair. Here you find the centre from an inline formula and place a bulky group correctly.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Full marks need correct tetrahedral geometry shown with wedge-dash.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The drawings must communicate 3D. Omitting wedge-dash caps the answer at one mark, even with sensible angles.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Using 90° bond angles, or changing two groups as well as wedge-dash; both were reported in 25M.2.HL.6221.4.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Omitting wedge-dash gives 1 max; 90° bond angles are not accepted.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: One mark: correct non-3D pair with proper angles. Two marks: the mirror-image pair also shows wedge-dash.

3_novel_application.short: The bulky C(CH3)3 is just one group on the centre.
3_novel_application.why: Chirality depends on four different attachments, not on their size, so a large group occupies one position like any other.
3_novel_application.avoid: Calling the C(CH3)3 carbon chiral; it has three identical methyl groups.
3_novel_application.disguise: An inline formula with a bracketed group hides which carbon is chiral.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Expand it; only a carbon with one H can pass here.

4_command_terms.why: Draw demands an accurate diagram, and this question specifically asks for orientation around the centre.
4_command_terms.demands: Two accurate 3D structures around the chiral centre.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Two marks for the correct 3D pair; one maximum without wedge-dash.

5_time_efficiency.short: Draw one carefully, then copy it in reverse.
5_time_efficiency.why: The second structure comes directly from the first, so reflecting is faster and safer than designing it again.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Drawing the second isomer from scratch.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Show the C(CH3)3 as a group; do not draw every C-H bond.

6_data_booklet.short: Wedge-dash drawing is not in the booklet sections provided.
6_data_booklet.why: The sections provided give spectral data. They do not show how to draw stereochemistry.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Searching for a template during the exam.
6_data_booklet.pattern: No table helps; this is a drawing routine.
6_data_booklet.memorise: The definition of a chiral carbon and wedge-dash conventions are NOT in the sections provided; memorise them.

7_elimination.short: Flat crosses and reflect-plus-swap pairs are out.
7_elimination.why: A swap undoes a reflection, leaving two drawings of the same molecule rather than a pair of enantiomers.
7_elimination.avoid: Checking only that the groups are correct, without comparing their positions.

definitely_wrong.rule: The markscheme rejects 90° bond angles.

definitely_wrong.target: A mirror image with two groups also swapped
definitely_wrong.rule: The drawing returns to the original molecule.

definitely_wrong.target: Centre placed on the C(CH3)3 carbon
definitely_wrong.rule: Three identical methyl groups cannot give four different groups.

walkthrough.answer: Two mirror-image tetrahedral wedge-dash structures centred on the CHBr carbon, with H, Br, CH3 and C(CH3)3 as its four groups.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.7 stereochemical formulas and enantiomers (AHL).
1_context.textbook_gap: Books present finished pairs; exams require you to locate the centre before drawing.

trap_boundaries: No wedge-dash: [1 max].
90° bond angles are not accepted.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: The second mark depends on showing 3D, not only correct connectivity.

disguises: The chiral centre is hidden in an inline formula.
A bulky group sits on the centre.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Expand first; test only carbons that could carry four different groups.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Marks for the 3D mirror-image pair, capped at one without wedge-dash.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Leave large substituents condensed.

6_data_booklet.hack: No help in the sections provided; memorise the wedge-dash routine.

rules: A 90° drawing is not accepted.
Reflecting and also swapping two groups gives identical structures, not enantiomers.

evidence.note: [1 max] without wedge-dash; 90° bond angles rejected.
About half drew these correctly; lists wrong centre, 90° angles, missing wedge-dash and identical structures.
Difficulty drawing 3D structures and showing the spatial relationship of enantiomers.
Weak grasp of 3D wedge-dash representations.

cards.difficulty_signal: About half succeeded in May 2025; drawing 3D isomers is flagged as difficult in several sessions.

cards.title: Molecular formula from M+: fixed atoms first, then the general formula

walkthrough.question: An ester's mass spectrum has its molecular ion at m/z 102. The ester has no rings and no multiple C-C bonds. Using relative atomic masses from the data booklet, deduce its molecular formula.
walkthrough.key_idea: Ester oxygen uses 32; the remaining 70 fits C5H10.
walkthrough.careful: Subtract all the group's atoms: an ester has two oxygens.
procedure: Write down atoms fixed by the functional group.
Subtract their mass from the molecular ion value.
Use the series pattern for the carbon and hydrogen.
Find n and write the full formula.
Add the atomic masses to check.
tricks: Each CH2 is about 14: divide the remaining mass by 14.
Fails if rings or C=C are present: each removes two H.
if_lost: Which atoms must every ester contain?
How much mass do those atoms use?
What mass is left for carbon and hydrogen?
What C:H ratio fits no rings or multiple bonds?

1_context.short: Link a molecular ion to a homologous-series formula.
1_context.why: M+ gives the total mass, while the series gives the atom pattern. Together they fix the formula.
1_context.avoid: Trying to read the formula directly from the mass number.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.8: deduce structural information from MS, including the molecular ion.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books usually start from percentage composition. Here the formula comes from M+ plus structural limits.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Show two oxygens and remaining mass 70, then give C5H10O2.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The first mark rewards recognising the ester's oxygen atoms. The second rewards the rest of the formula.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Using one oxygen or giving a formula without working; few showed the derivation in 03M.2.HL.TZ0.9.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: The correct final formula earns both marks; a wrong formula needs visible two-oxygen working for one.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial: shows two O and 70 only. Full: reaches C5H10O2.

3_novel_application.short: No rings and no multiple bonds means CnH2n plus group atoms.
3_novel_application.why: Those limits rule out missing hydrogen pairs, so the remaining carbon and hydrogen must fit the saturated ester pattern.
3_novel_application.avoid: Ignoring the structural limits and trying many C and H combinations.
3_novel_application.disguise: A spectrum statement is really a mass-balance problem.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Mass minus group atoms equals the carbon-hydrogen part.

4_command_terms.short: Deduce: reach the formula from the given facts.
4_command_terms.why: Deduce requires a conclusion from the information, so the given mass and ester identity must be used.
4_command_terms.avoid: Writing a guessed ester formula without using 102.
4_command_terms.demands: A molecular formula derived from M+ and the structural limits.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: M1 shows two oxygens; M2 gives the formula; correct final answer scores 2.

5_time_efficiency.short: Subtract 32, divide by 14, then write the formula.
5_time_efficiency.why: The general pattern avoids trial and error and gives the formula in two short operations.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Calculating an empirical formula first; no percentage data are given.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not draw the ester unless a later part asks.

6_data_booklet.short: Atomic masses come from section 7; the ester formula does not.
6_data_booklet.why: The question points to section 7 for masses, but the family pattern is knowledge you bring yourself.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Expecting a table of general formulas.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Read C, H and O atomic masses as the question directs.
6_data_booklet.memorise: CnH2nO2 for saturated non-cyclic esters is NOT in the booklet sections provided; memorise it.

7_elimination.short: One oxygen or odd hydrogen counts cannot be right.
7_elimination.why: The ester group fixes two oxygens, and a neutral C, H and O compound always has an even hydrogen count.
7_elimination.avoid: Accepting a formula merely because its mass is close to 102.

definitely_wrong.rule: An ester group contains two oxygen atoms.
A neutral C, H and O molecule has even H.
No rings or multiple C-C bonds gives this ratio for this ester.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.3 general formulas with S3.2.8 molecular ion.
1_context.textbook_gap: Exams begin from a spectrum and structural limits, not percentage composition.

trap_boundaries: Correct final formula earns [2].
Working must demonstrate the two oxygens for M1 if the final formula is wrong.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Identifying the oxygen count earns M1; completing C and H earns M2.

disguises: Mass spectrum in a synthesis question.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Mass minus group atoms equals CnH2n when there are no rings or multiple bonds.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Method mark then formula mark; correct final answer gets both.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not attempt empirical-formula work without percentages.

6_data_booklet.hack: Use section 7 only for masses, as the question directs; the ester pattern is not supplied.

rules: Reject one-oxygen formulas for an ester.
Reject odd hydrogen counts for a neutral C, H and O molecule.

evidence.note: M1 demonstrates two oxygens and 70; M2 gives C5H10O2.
Molecular ion 102 with no rings or multiple C-C bonds.
Few candidates showed how they derived the molecular formula.
About 20% found a molecular formula correctly from a drawn structure; hydrogen counting was the problem.

cards.difficulty_signal: No percentage reported for this item; formula work from structures reached only about 20% on a 2025 Paper 2 question.

cards.title: IR from the table: pair each peak with its bond

walkthrough.question: A student makes an ester and records its IR spectrum. The graph is not shown here. Using section 20 of the data booklet, identify two absorptions, each with wavenumber and bond, that confirm an ester.
walkthrough.key_idea: An ester contains C=O and C-O; read both ranges from section 20.
walkthrough.careful: Pair every wavenumber with its bond.
procedure: List the bonds in the named functional group.
Find each bond's row in section 20.
Give a wavenumber in range with its bond.
Check the peak on any printed spectrum.
Note any expected peaks that are absent.
tricks: No broad 2500-3000 O-H helps rule out a carboxylic acid.
Check that the atoms in your bond are actually in the compound.
if_lost: Which two kinds of carbon-oxygen bond does an ester contain?
Which table in the booklet lists bond absorptions?
Which rows of that table include esters?

1_context.short: Confirm a functional group using two bonds, not one peak.
1_context.why: C=O alone also occurs in aldehydes, ketones and acids, so an ester is confirmed by adding the C-O bond.
1_context.avoid: Stopping at C=O because it is usually the most obvious peak.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.9: interpret the functional group region of an IR spectrum using a frequency table.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books label one peak at a time; this question needs the pair of peaks that together fit the group.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Each line needs a value in range and the bond.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Wavenumber and bond are joined in the markscheme, so a value or a bond alone does not complete a peak.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Naming groups but not wavenumbers; this was reported in 18M.3.HL.TZ1.16 and 04N.2.HL.TZ0.6.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Any value in the range and either order are accepted.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Full credit: two complete wavenumber-and-bond pairs. Partial: one complete pair.

3_novel_application.short: The named group tells you which rows to read.
3_novel_application.why: The table is organised by bond and molecule type, so the expected peaks are found before reading the graph.
3_novel_application.avoid: Reading every peak and trying to match each one.
3_novel_application.disguise: A crowded spectrum suggests every peak must be assigned.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Start from the group's bonds, then look for only those peaks.

4_command_terms.short: Deduce: choose the peaks and state their bonds.
4_command_terms.why: Deduce requires a conclusion from the table and spectrum, not a general definition of IR.
4_command_terms.avoid: Writing a description of how IR spectroscopy works.
4_command_terms.demands: Two peak values with the bond responsible for each.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark for each complete wavenumber-and-bond pair.

5_time_efficiency.short: Two rows, two lines, then move on.
5_time_efficiency.why: Only two pairs earn marks, so assigning extra peaks costs time without adding credit.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Assigning fingerprint-region peaks you were not asked about.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip C-H peaks; they do not confirm an ester.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 20 lists both ester bonds and their ranges.
6_data_booklet.why: The table names esters in both the C=O and C-O rows, so the answer can be read rather than memorised.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Using a remembered value outside the printed range.
6_data_booklet.pattern: C=O 1700-1750 and C-O 1050-1410 both list esters.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Which bonds an ester contains is NOT printed as a structure; recognise -COO- yourself.

7_elimination.short: Bonds absent from an ester cannot confirm it.
7_elimination.why: A peak can only be assigned to a bond the molecule could contain, so the formula limits the choices.
7_elimination.avoid: Choosing C-F or N-H from a nearby row; such errors were reported in 25M.2.HL.6221.1.

definitely_wrong.rule: The ester contains no fluorine.
The ester contains no nitrogen.
The ester group has no O-H bond.

walkthrough.answer: C=O at 1700-1750 cm⁻¹ and C-O at 1050-1410 cm⁻¹, in either order.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.9 functional group region with data booklet section 20.
1_context.textbook_gap: Exams ask for the bonds that confirm a group, not a complete spectrum assignment.

trap_boundaries: Any value in the given range is accepted.
Either order is accepted.
Candidates must identify the bond responsible, not only the group (04M.2.HL.TZ0.11).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A complete pair scores; a wavenumber or bond alone leaves the peak incomplete.

disguises: A question about what is absent rather than present.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Predict the peaks from the bonds before reading the spectrum.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark per complete pair; the absent-bond part needs both range and bond.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Ignore peaks that do not distinguish the requested group.

6_data_booklet.hack: The table's molecule-type column tells you which rows apply to esters.

rules: Reject bonds containing atoms absent from the compound.
An ester has no O-H bond; a broad acid O-H peak would point to another group or impurity.

evidence.note: Peak pairs require wavenumber and bond; any order and any value in range.
Directs students to section 20 to confirm an ester.
Groups were identified without absorption wavenumbers.
Bonds were identified but frequencies were often omitted.
C-F and N-H were given though those bonds were not in the molecule.

cards.difficulty_signal: Bond identification is often well prepared, but marks are lost through incomplete pairs and impossible bonds.

cards.title: NMR ratios: a 6 means two equivalent methyl groups

walkthrough.question:
An alcohol, C4H9OH, gives four 1H NMR signals with areas in the ratio 6:2:1:1. Which alcohol is it?
A. Butan-1-ol
B. Butan-2-ol
C. 2-methylpropan-1-ol
D. 2-methylpropan-2-ol
walkthrough.key_idea: A 6 requires two identical CH3 groups, and the remaining hydrogens must give 2:1:1.
walkthrough.question_type: 1H NMR: match isomer to peak ratio
walkthrough.careful: Hydrogens on different carbons are equivalent only with matching surroundings.
procedure: Draw each candidate's full structure.
Group hydrogens by chemical environment.
Count the hydrogens in each environment.
Compare the number of signals with the data.
Compare the ratio with the data.
tricks: Look for the largest ratio number first; a 6 suggests two equivalent methyls.
Count signals first; the wrong number removes an isomer without checking the ratio.
if_lost: What does each number in the ratio count?
How could one signal contain six hydrogens?
Which isomers could have two equivalent methyl groups?
How many environments does each remaining isomer have?

1_context.short: Choose among isomers from NMR areas, without a printed spectrum.
1_context.why: Area ratios come directly from counting equivalent hydrogens in the structure, so a spectrum is not needed.
1_context.avoid: Thinking this cannot be done without seeing a graph; 07M.1.HL.TZ0.38 addressed this point.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.10: deduce structures from the number of signals and relative areas.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books begin with one structure and predict its spectrum. Here you test four isomers against one ratio.

2_markscheme_logic.short: One letter only: signals and ratio must both match.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Multiple isomers may have some matching features, but only one structure fits four signals and the exact ratio.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Guessing among similar names; wrong answers were spread evenly in 25M.1A.HL.6219.18.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: A correct signal count alone is not enough without the exact ratio.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Right answer: 6, 2, 1 and 1 hydrogens. Tempting butan-2-ol: five signals with no 6.

3_novel_application.short: Names conceal the symmetry that decides the ratio.
3_novel_application.why: Equivalent groups share one signal and add their hydrogens together, so symmetry appears only after drawing.
3_novel_application.avoid: Counting CH2 groups in different positions as one environment, as reported in 05M.2.HL.TZ0.9.
3_novel_application.disguise: Four similar names replace the structures you need.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Convert each name to a structure, then read the largest area.

4_command_terms.short: No command term: an MCQ stem needs identification.
4_command_terms.why: Only the final letter is marked, so short sketches are useful only if they speed elimination.
4_command_terms.avoid: Writing out full chemical shift predictions.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Use the 6 first, then confirm the rest.
5_time_efficiency.why: The 6 removes most structures immediately, leaving only a short check of the remaining environments.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Using chemical shift values not provided or needed.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip the shift table; the ratio decides this one.

6_data_booklet.short: No section is needed; count hydrogens in each environment.
6_data_booklet.why: The shift table describes signal positions, whereas this question depends on signal areas.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Opening section 21 when no chemical shifts are given.
6_data_booklet.pattern: The ratio comes from the structure, not a table.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Signal area is proportional to the number of equivalent hydrogens; this is NOT in the sections provided.

7_elimination.short: Only one option can make exactly 6 equivalent methyl hydrogens.
7_elimination.why: The 6 needs two equivalent CH3 groups. Straight chains and three-methyl structures cannot give that area.
7_elimination.avoid: Treating the two CH3 groups in butan-2-ol as equivalent.

definitely_wrong.rule: Butan-1-ol has no two equivalent CH3 groups.
Its two CH3 groups are in different environments.
Three equivalent CH3 groups give an area of 9.

walkthrough.answer: C. 2-methylpropan-1-ol: (CH3)2CHCH2OH has environments containing 6, 1, 2 and 1 hydrogens.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.10 number of signals and relative areas.
1_context.textbook_gap: Exams require a comparison of isomers, not one prediction from one drawn molecule.

trap_boundaries: For the structured version, ratios may be accepted in any order where stated (25M.2.HL.6209.8).
For an MCQ, only the exact matching structure earns the mark.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A matching signal count is partial reasoning; the exact area pattern identifies the isomer.

3_novel_application.heuristic: Draw, group equivalent hydrogens, then compare the largest area first.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ one mark; structured questions may split signals and areas.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Ignore chemical shift when only areas are given.

6_data_booklet.hack: Use section 21 only when chemical shifts are given; areas come from your hydrogen count.

rules: A 6 cannot arise without equivalent groups totalling six hydrogens.
Three equivalent methyl groups make a 9, not a 6.

evidence.note: Answer C for ratio 6:2:1:1.
Under 50% correct; wrong answers spread across all distractors.
Structured NMR marks for number of signals and relative areas.
Peak-area ratios can be found from a condensed formula without a spectrum.
Too few peaks given by treating different CH2 hydrogens as equivalent.

cards.difficulty_signal: Under 50% correct in May 2025; predicting signals and relative areas is flagged as difficult.

cards.title: Name from an inline formula: expand, then find the chain

walkthrough.question: Substance X is a halogenoalkane with the condensed formula CH3CHBrC(CH3)3. Give its IUPAC name.
walkthrough.key_idea: Expand the formula: four-carbon chain with lowest locants 2,2,3.
walkthrough.careful: Identical branches need di and one locant each.
procedure: Draw the structure from the condensed formula.
Find the longest continuous carbon chain.
Number from the end giving lowest locants.
List substituents alphabetically, ignoring di and tri.
Give every substituent its own locant.
tricks: C(CH3)3 hides one chain carbon and two methyl branches.
Check: carbons in the name must equal carbons in the formula.
if_lost: What does C(CH3)3 look like when drawn?
Which path through the carbons is longest?
Which numbering direction gives the smallest locants?
Which substituent name comes first alphabetically?

1_context.short: Name a branched halogenoalkane from an inline formula, not a drawing.
1_context.why: The formula conceals the branching, so finding the longest chain is the first task rather than a given.
1_context.avoid: Assuming the carbons written in a row form the main chain.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.5: apply IUPAC names to saturated compounds, up to six parent carbons, including branched isomers.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books usually name drawn skeletons. Examiners reported the extra inline-to-structure step as a real barrier.

2_markscheme_logic.short: One mark requires the complete name, including di and locants.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The single mark is for the name itself, so each reported error directly threatens the only available mark.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Omitting di, omitting a second methyl locant, or misidentifying the chain, as reported in 25M.2.HL.6221.4.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: The mark stops when the locants, di or parent chain are wrong.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Full credit has parent butane and 2,2-dimethyl. Zero follows from a wrong parent or incomplete locant set.

3_novel_application.short: The bracket looks like one branch but contains chain and branches.
3_novel_application.why: One methyl from the bracket can continue the longest chain, while the other two become branches.
3_novel_application.avoid: Treating C(CH3)3 as a single substituent on a shorter chain.
3_novel_application.disguise: A compact bracketed group hides where the chain runs.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Expand any bracket, then trace the longest end-to-end path.

4_command_terms.short: State: the name only, without reasoning.
4_command_terms.why: State requires a brief answer, so the mark comes from the final name, not from the sketch.
4_command_terms.avoid: Leaving several possible names on the line.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Sketch the carbons, number them, write the name.
5_time_efficiency.why: A carbon skeleton shows the chain and locants; drawn hydrogens do not change the name.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Leave hydrogens off your rough sketch.

6_data_booklet.short: Naming rules are not in the booklet sections provided.
6_data_booklet.why: The sections provided contain spectral data, so nomenclature rules must be recalled.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking for a naming table during the exam.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Parent stems, di and tri prefixes, alphabetical order and lowest locants are NOT in the sections provided.

7_elimination.short: A dimethyl compound without di cannot be right.
7_elimination.why: These checks use only counting, so they reject poor names before numbering them.
7_elimination.avoid: Trusting a name because it sounds complete.

definitely_wrong.target: A name not totalling six carbons
definitely_wrong.rule: X contains six carbon atoms.
Two identical methyl branches need the prefix.
The longest chain has only four carbons.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.5 IUPAC nomenclature, including branched chains.
1_context.textbook_gap: Exams often add a formula-to-structure step before naming.

trap_boundaries: Missing di or a missing methyl locant loses the name.
A wrong longest chain leads to a wrong parent.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: The only mark is the complete name.

disguises: Branches that continue the longest chain.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Draw the carbons first, then find the parent.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Usually one mark for the entire name.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not draw hydrogens.

6_data_booklet.hack: No nomenclature table appears in the sections provided; memorise the rules.

rules: A name's carbon count must match the formula.
Two identical branches require di.

evidence.note: Name credited as 3-bromo-2,2-dimethylbutane for one mark.
40% correct; missing di, missing locant and wrong chain reported.
Students struggled to move from inline formula to structure and find the longest chain.
Misnumbered chains and omitted branches were reported.

cards.difficulty_signal: 40% correct on this item in May 2025.

cards.title: Reject impossible names: chain, locant and prefix errors

walkthrough.question:
A branched aldehyde is drawn in the paper. The drawing is not needed here: only one name obeys IUPAC rules. Which name is it?
A. 2,3-dimethylpentanal
B. 2,3-methylpentanal
C. 2-methyl-3-ethylbutanal
D. 3-ethyl-2-methylbutanal
walkthrough.key_idea: An ethyl on C3 of butanal means the true chain is longer.
walkthrough.careful: The parent must be the longest chain with the group.
procedure: Find the longest chain containing the functional group carbon.
Number so the main group has the lowest number.
Name and locate every branch.
Order branches alphabetically, with di or tri where needed.
tricks: Ethyl on the second-to-last carbon: a longer chain exists, so reject.
Aldehyde and acid carbons are always C1; check the name respects this.
if_lost: What prefix do two identical branches need?
How long is the chain if you continue through an ethyl group?
Which substituent should come first alphabetically?

1_context.short: Choose a valid IUPAC name by testing naming rules.
1_context.why: Each distractor breaks a separate rule, so the rules themselves can remove them even without the structure.
1_context.avoid: Thinking the question is impossible because no drawing appears.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.5: apply IUPAC names to branched carbonyl compounds up to six parent carbons.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books generate one name from a structure. MCQs test whether you can spot a broken rule in a name.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Only the longest parent with correct prefixes survives.
2_markscheme_logic.why: C and D describe a chain that can be extended, while B omits the required prefix.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Omitting di or choosing too short a chain; both errors were reported in 25M.2.SL.TZ3.4.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: An attractive alphabetical name still fails if its parent chain is too short.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Tempting D is correctly alphabetical, but its chain is too short. A uses the longest chain.

3_novel_application.short: Options hide one structure behind several invalid names.
3_novel_application.why: C and D would be drawn as the same structure as A, but a longer parent chain makes their names invalid.
3_novel_application.avoid: Assuming a name is valid simply because you can draw it.
3_novel_application.disguise: Long option names look equally professional.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask whether any branch could extend the parent chain.

4_command_terms.short: No command term: an MCQ stem needs identification.
4_command_terms.why: Only one valid name is credited, so rule testing is more useful than complete drafting.
4_command_terms.avoid: Spending time drawing all four options fully.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Use prefix, chain and alphabetical checks in that order.
5_time_efficiency.why: These checks need no calculation and can remove options one at a time quickly.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Trying to draw every structure first.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not draw the correct option once the others are rejected.

6_data_booklet.short: This needs naming rules, not a booklet table.
6_data_booklet.why: The sections provided have spectral data rather than IUPAC conventions.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking for a naming pattern in section 21.
6_data_booklet.memorise: IUPAC prefixes, parent stems and locant rules are NOT in the sections provided.

7_elimination.short: Three distractors fail on prefix or chain length.
7_elimination.why: The rules are structural and do not require any calculation.
7_elimination.avoid: Keeping C because its substituents appear in locant order rather than alphabetical order.

definitely_wrong.rule: Two methyl groups require the prefix di.
The ethyl group extends the parent; substituents are also non-alphabetical.
The ethyl on C3 gives a longer parent chain.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.5 IUPAC nomenclature.
1_context.textbook_gap: MCQ distractors reward checking broken rules, not only generating a name.

trap_boundaries: A valid-looking alkyl order does not rescue a parent chain that is too short.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: The correct option satisfies all rules; each distractor breaks at least one.

disguises: Same structure named several wrong ways.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Test whether any branch can continue the parent chain.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark for one letter.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not draw options already rejected.

6_data_booklet.hack: No nomenclature table appears in the sections provided.

rules: Two identical branches without di are invalid.
Aldehyde and carboxylic acid carbons take locant 1.

evidence.note: Answer A: 2,3-dimethylpentanal.
Longest-chain and di errors reported.
47.5% correct; lowest locant should go on the ketone group.
Same type with an acid group in the distractors.

cards.difficulty_signal: No percentage for this item; similar ketone naming reached 47.5%.

cards.title: Stereoisomers: test cis-trans and chirality, not just one

walkthrough.question:
Which of these could exist as stereoisomers?
I. CH2=CClBr
II. CHBrICl
III. CHBr=CClBr
A. I and II only
B. I and III only
C. II and III only
D. I, II and III
walkthrough.key_idea: Stereoisomers: restricted C=C with different pairs, or a carbon with four different groups.
walkthrough.careful: Each double-bond carbon must carry two different groups.
procedure: Sort each compound by C=C or four single bonds.
For C=C, list the two groups on each carbon.
Cis-trans requires two different groups on each carbon.
For a single-bonded carbon, check for four different groups.
Either test passing means stereoisomers can exist.
tricks: A =CH2 or =CX2 end stops cis-trans immediately.
Different groups are needed per carbon; both carbons may share one group.
if_lost: Which types of stereoisomerism are in the syllabus?
Which formulas have a carbon-carbon double bond?
What groups are on each carbon of that double bond?
Which formula has one carbon bonded to four atoms?

1_context.short: Stereoisomer covers both cis-trans and optical isomerism.
1_context.why: Both have the same connectivity but different spatial arrangements, so each compound needs testing against both criteria.
1_context.avoid: Answering only with cis-trans in mind.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.7: stereoisomers include cis-trans isomerism and chiral carbon atoms giving optical isomers.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach the types separately. This item mixes them in one list and uses the umbrella word.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Each listed compound must correctly pass or fail.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The combination options mean one wrong judgement moves you to a wrong answer, even when the others are right.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Overlooking a two-identical-group end; 37% and 25% chose wrong options in 25M.1A.HL.6213.17.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: One identical pair on either double-bond carbon removes cis-trans.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Tempting I fails at its CH2 end. III passes because each carbon has different groups.

3_novel_application.short: A one-carbon halomethane can still be chiral.
3_novel_application.why: Four different atoms on one carbon are enough; chirality does not need a long molecule.
3_novel_application.avoid: Dismissing CHBrICl because it looks too small.
3_novel_application.disguise: Small halogen formulas hide a chiral carbon and a cis-trans alkene.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask: restricted double bond or four different groups?

4_command_terms.short: No command term: an MCQ stem needs yes-or-no decisions.
4_command_terms.why: Each statement can be checked separately, then matched to the combination options.
4_command_terms.avoid: Reading the option groups before testing the statements.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Check I first; its CH2 end removes three options.
5_time_efficiency.why: Starting with the quickest structural failure removes several combinations before the other formulas are tested.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Writing wedge-dash structures for an MCQ.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not draw the isomers.

6_data_booklet.short: Stereoisomer rules are not in the booklet sections provided.
6_data_booklet.why: The sections provided contain spectral data and do not state structural conditions for isomerism.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking up isomer rules during the exam.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Cis-trans and chiral-carbon criteria are NOT in the sections provided.

7_elimination.short: CH2= means I fails, so all options containing I go.
7_elimination.why: Two H atoms on one double-bond carbon make the swapped arrangement identical, so cis-trans cannot occur.
7_elimination.avoid: Marking CHBr=CClBr wrong because Br appears on both carbons.

definitely_wrong.rule: It includes I, whose CH2 carbon has identical hydrogens.
It includes I, whose CH2 carbon has identical hydrogens.
It includes I, whose CH2 carbon has identical hydrogens.

walkthrough.answer: C. II has a chiral carbon; III has different groups on each double-bond carbon.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.7 stereoisomerism: cis-trans and chiral centres.
1_context.textbook_gap: Exams mix types and use skeletal or minimal formulas.

trigger_phrases: two nonidentical groups on each doubly bonded carbon
trap_boundaries: Identical groups on one double-bond carbon prevent cis-trans.
Answers defining chiral carbon through optical properties were not accepted in 25M.2.HL.6215.4.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Checking only one double-bond carbon can make a compound falsely pass.

3_novel_application.heuristic: Test both stereoisomer routes for every compound.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ one mark; written questions may separately credit the feature and reason.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not draw isomers unless asked.

6_data_booklet.hack: No stereochemistry rule appears in the sections provided.

rules: A =CH2 or =CX2 end cannot show cis-trans.
Sharing one group across the two carbons does not prevent cis-trans if each carbon has different groups.

evidence.note: Answer C: II and III.
Correct answer B in a cis-trans item with skeletal options.
22% correct; two different groups are needed on each double-bond carbon.
Chiral carbon defined by four different atoms or groups.

cards.difficulty_signal: A closely related May 2025 cis-trans MCQ was the hardest item in its paper at 22% correct.

cards.title: Chiral centre: compare all four groups

walkthrough.question:
Which molecule has a chiral centre?
A. CH3CH(CH3)CHO
B. CH3CHClCH2CH3
C. CH3C(CH3)2OH
D. ClCH2CH2COOH
walkthrough.key_idea: A chiral carbon must be bonded to four different atoms or groups.
walkthrough.careful: Compare whole groups, not just the first attached atom.
procedure: Ignore CH3, CH2 and doubly bonded carbons.
List the four groups on each remaining carbon.
Compare each complete group along the chain.
Call it chiral only if all four differ.
tricks: Check ring-side-chain junction carbons; these were missed in a past item.
n chiral centres give up to 2ⁿ optical isomers.
if_lost: Which carbons can be ignored immediately?
What four groups are on each remaining carbon?
Are any two of those groups identical?

1_context.short: Spot a chiral centre by reading a condensed formula.
1_context.why: The criterion is structural and uses connectivity, so the condensed formula must be read like a diagram.
1_context.avoid: Looking for an unusual functional group instead of four different groups.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.7: a chiral carbon gives rise to stereoisomers with different optical properties.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books mark chiral carbons on drawings; here you unpack each condensed formula first.

2_markscheme_logic.short: The test is four different atoms or groups.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Optical behaviour is a consequence of chirality, not the definition requested for a chiral carbon.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Defining a chiral carbon only by optical activity; 25M.2.HL.6215.4 does not accept this.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Answers referring only to optical properties do not earn the definition mark.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Correct B has H, Cl, CH3 and C2H5. Tempting A has two CH3 groups.

3_novel_application.short: Brackets can hide two identical methyl groups.
3_novel_application.why: Writing a group in brackets does not make it different from a neighbouring identical group.
3_novel_application.avoid: Thinking the bracketed CH3 in option A differs from the first CH3.
3_novel_application.disguise: Condensed formulas put identical groups in different places.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Rewrite each candidate carbon's four attachments as a list.

4_command_terms.short: No command term: an MCQ stem needs one structure.
4_command_terms.why: Only the final letter is marked, so short attachment lists are enough for the check.
4_command_terms.avoid: Drawing all four molecules in full.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Check only carbons that carry one hydrogen or none.
5_time_efficiency.why: CH3 and CH2 carbons have repeated hydrogens, so they cannot be chiral and need no further checking.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not draw 3D shapes for this identification.

6_data_booklet.short: The chiral-centre rule is not in the sections provided.
6_data_booklet.why: The sections provided contain spectral data and do not define chirality.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking for a chiral-centre rule in the data sections.
6_data_booklet.memorise: The four-different-groups rule is NOT in the sections provided.

7_elimination.short: Repeated CH3 or only CH2 groups remove three options.
7_elimination.why: A duplicate attachment immediately rules out chirality at that carbon, so calculation is unnecessary.
7_elimination.avoid: Calling the carbonyl carbon chiral; it has only three attachments.

definitely_wrong.rule: Its only candidate carbon has two CH3 groups.
Its central carbon has three CH3 groups.
It has only CH2 carbons and a COOH carbon.

walkthrough.answer: B. Its second carbon has H, Cl, CH3 and C2H5.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.7 chiral carbon atoms and optical isomers.
1_context.textbook_gap: Exams hide the centre in condensed formulas, rings or side-chain junctions.

trigger_phrases: not superimposable on its mirror image
trap_boundaries: Answers relying only on optical properties are not accepted for this definition.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Listing four attachments prevents counting a chiral carbon when two groups match.

3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask for each candidate carbon: what are its four attachments?

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ one mark; definition questions one mark.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip full stereo drawings when only identification is needed.

6_data_booklet.hack: No help in the sections provided.

rules: CH3 and CH2 carbons cannot be chiral centres.
A doubly bonded carbon cannot be a chiral centre.

evidence.note: Answer B.
Four different atoms or groups; optical-property answers not accepted.
About 45% correctly counted three centres from a skeletal formula.
Two centres give four isomers; many missed the ring-side-chain centre.

cards.difficulty_signal: Counting centres in large skeletal molecules reached about 45% in May 2025 and just over half in November 2024.

cards.title: Optically active product: react first, then test chirality

walkthrough.question:
Which compound forms an optically active product when reduced with LiAlH4?
A. Propanal
B. Butanal
C. Butanone
D. Propanone
walkthrough.key_idea: Reduce each carbonyl, then seek a carbon with four different groups.
walkthrough.careful: Test the product, not the starting carbonyl compound.
procedure: Write the product of the stated reaction.
Find the carbon that changed in the reaction.
List that carbon's four attached groups.
Call the product chiral only if all differ.
tricks: Aldehyde gives CH2OH, not chiral there. Fails if another carbon is chiral.
A symmetric ketone gives two identical R groups, so no new chiral centre.
if_lost: What functional group does LiAlH4 produce from a carbonyl?
Which product has a carbon carrying OH and H?
What four groups are on that carbon?

1_context.short: The chirality test comes after an organic reaction.
1_context.why: The reaction creates the carbon that matters, so examining the reactant asks the wrong question.
1_context.avoid: Looking for a chiral centre in the carbonyl compound.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.7: a chiral carbon gives stereoisomers with different optical properties.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books test chirality on a finished molecule. This item adds a preliminary reaction step.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Only butanone's product has four different groups on the CHOH carbon.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Butan-2-ol has H, OH, CH3 and C2H5 on the changed carbon; the others have duplicate groups.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Picking an aldehyde because its name appears more reactive or complex.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Propanone also gives a secondary alcohol, but its two CH3 groups prevent chirality.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Right: butanone gives unequal R groups. Tempting propanone gives two identical methyl groups.

3_novel_application.short: A reduction question is really a chirality question.
3_novel_application.why: The reagent is only the route to the structure; the marked idea is symmetry at the changed carbon.
3_novel_application.avoid: Spending time on the reduction mechanism.
3_novel_application.disguise: The reagent LiAlH4 moves attention to reactions.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask: after reaction, what four groups surround the carbon?

4_command_terms.short: No command term: an MCQ stem needs one reactant.
4_command_terms.why: Only the identity of the correct starting compound is marked.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the reactant giving a chiral product.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Classify aldehyde or ketone, then check R groups.
5_time_efficiency.why: Aldehydes form CH2OH at the changed carbon, and ketones need a check for unequal R groups.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Writing full product structures for aldehydes.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip the mechanism and redox balancing.

6_data_booklet.short: Reduction products and chirality rules are not in provided sections.
6_data_booklet.why: The sections provided contain spectral data and no reaction scheme.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Searching data tables for reaction outcomes.
6_data_booklet.memorise: LiAlH4 reduction products and the chirality test are NOT in the sections provided.

7_elimination.short: Aldehydes and symmetric ketones cannot create this chiral centre.
7_elimination.why: An aldehyde product has two hydrogens on the changed carbon, and propanone gives two equal methyl groups.
7_elimination.avoid: Forgetting that a real reduction forms a racemic mixture; the item is asking whether the product is chiral.

definitely_wrong.rule: Propanal gives a CH2OH carbon with two hydrogens.
Butanal gives a CH2OH carbon with two hydrogens.
Propanone gives a product with two identical CH3 groups.

walkthrough.answer: C. Butanone gives butan-2-ol, whose CHOH carbon has H, OH, CH3 and C2H5. A real sample forms as a racemic mixture; the question means a chiral product.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.7 chiral carbon and optical properties.
1_context.textbook_gap: Exams link chirality to a reaction outcome, not just a static structure.

trap_boundaries: A secondary alcohol is not automatically chiral.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Unequal R groups on the ketone give chirality; equal R groups do not.

disguises: Starting molecule with no chiral centre.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Do the reaction, then apply the normal chirality test.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark for one letter.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not write the mechanism.

6_data_booklet.hack: No reaction or chirality table in the sections provided.

rules: Aldehyde reduction gives CH2OH at that carbon; this fails if a different chiral carbon exists.
A symmetric ketone gives two identical R groups.

evidence.note: Answer C: butanone.
About 63% deduced the carbonyl compound giving an optically active product.
Chirality defined by four different atoms or groups.

cards.title: Molecular ion: gives Mr, but is not always the tallest or most stable

walkthrough.question:
Consider these statements about the molecular ion, M+.
I. It need not be the tallest peak in the spectrum.
II. It is always the most stable fragment produced.
III. Its m/z value gives the molecule's relative molecular mass.
Which statements are correct?
A. I and II only
B. I and III only
C. II and III only
D. I, II and III
walkthrough.key_idea: M+ gives Mr, but it is not guaranteed tallest or most stable.
walkthrough.careful: Tallest peak and molecular ion are not the same thing.
procedure: Judge each statement separately as true or false.
Test the words always and never carefully.
Remember M+ is the ionised, unfragmented molecule.
Choose the option listing only true statements.
tricks: Always in a statement is a warning: look for one exception.
M+ can fragment, so a fragment may give the tallest peak.
if_lost: What does M+ tell you about the whole molecule?
Can M+ break into smaller pieces?
Must the peak for M+ be the tallest one?

1_context.short: Test what M+ does and does not guarantee.
1_context.why: M+ reports the intact molecule's mass, but peak height and stability are separate issues.
1_context.avoid: Treating the molecular ion as the most important peak in every sense.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.8: MS can fragment organic molecules; include the molecular ion.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books usually use M+ to find Mr. This tests its limits as well.

2_markscheme_logic.short: I and III are correct; II fails on the word always.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The M+ ion can fragment, so it is not always most stable, while its m/z still gives Mr.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Believing M+ is the most stable fragment, the key misconception in 24N.1.HL.TZ0.38.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Statement II breaks because it claims this is always true.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Correct B rejects II. Tempting D accepts a statement that merely sounds plausible.

3_novel_application.short: The word always changes a possible fact into a false claim.
3_novel_application.why: One counterexample disproves an absolute statement, so you need not rank every fragment's stability.
3_novel_application.avoid: Reading the statement as often rather than always.
3_novel_application.disguise: A plausible stability claim sits among correct mass facts.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Underline absolutes, then seek an exception.

4_command_terms.short: No command term: an MCQ stem needs statement judgement.
4_command_terms.why: Combination options reward knowing exactly which statements hold, not partial familiarity.
4_command_terms.avoid: Choosing D just because all statements sound familiar.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Reject II, then B follows if I and III hold.
5_time_efficiency.why: Three of the four options contain II, so one secure judgement removes most of the paper's choices.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Calculating masses; no numbers are provided.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip fragment calculations; this is a concept item.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 22 lists mass losses, not molecular-ion properties.
6_data_booklet.why: The table helps interpret fragments but does not state whether M+ is tallest or most stable.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking for these statements in the mass-lost table.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Use section 22 for losses such as 15 or 29 when m/z values are given.
6_data_booklet.memorise: What M+ represents and its limits are NOT stated in section 22.

7_elimination.short: Any option containing II can be rejected.
7_elimination.why: M+ can fragment during electron bombardment, so stability is not guaranteed.
7_elimination.avoid: Leaving in A or D because II sounds like a simple summary.

definitely_wrong.rule: It contains statement II.
It contains statement II.
It contains statement II.

M+ is not necessarily the most stable species.
Older reports penalised missing + charges on ions, for example 09N.3.HL.TZ0.2; one 2024 SL session did not (24N.2.SL.TZ0.4).

cards.title: IR limits: bond type yes, bond position no

walkthrough.question:
What is a limitation of infrared spectroscopy?
A. It cannot detect small atoms such as H.
B. It reveals only the molar mass.
C. It changes the sample's chemical structure.
D. It identifies bonds but not where they are.
walkthrough.key_idea: IR identifies bond types, but gives no bond position.
walkthrough.question_type: Analytical technique: what it can show
walkthrough.careful: IR does detect bonds to hydrogen, such as O-H.
procedure: Recall what the technique measures.
Match each option to the correct technique.
Reject claims belonging to another technique.
Choose the true limitation of this technique.
tricks: Molar mass suggests MS; hydrogen environments suggest NMR; bond type suggests IR.
The same C=O range covers several classes, so IR cannot give full structure.
if_lost: What does an IR absorption tell you about?
Which technique would give molar mass?
Does a peak show where a bond sits in the molecule?

1_context.short: Know what IR cannot tell you.
1_context.why: Techniques are combined because each gives different evidence; IR identifies bonds and leaves structural position uncertain.
1_context.avoid: Treating IR as a complete structure-determination method.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.9: IR identifies the type of bond present in a molecule.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books emphasise what IR identifies. This asks what remains unknown after reading the peaks.

2_markscheme_logic.short: The correct limitation is bond identification without position.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The peak ranges link to bond types, not to specific locations in the molecule.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Giving a limitation that actually describes another technique.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Molar mass belongs to mass spectrometry, not IR.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Correct D describes IR's real limit. Tempting B swaps IR with MS.

3_novel_application.short: A disadvantage question tests the purpose of each technique.
3_novel_application.why: Knowing what each method measures lets you recognise claims that belong to a different method.
3_novel_application.avoid: Choosing a statement merely because it sounds negative.
3_novel_application.disguise: Negative wording replaces a direct bond-identification question.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask: what does this method actually measure?

4_command_terms.short: No command term: an MCQ stem needs one limitation.
4_command_terms.why: Only the true limitation earns the mark, so a general knowledge of IR is not enough.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Assign each false claim to another technique.
5_time_efficiency.why: This turns recall into quick elimination and avoids debating vague disadvantages.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Considering instrument details the options never mention.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip theory of how IR is absorbed.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 20 shows one C=O range across several molecule types.
6_data_booklet.why: A shared range illustrates that a bond can be identified without revealing exactly where or in which structure it sits.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Thinking one range identifies only one compound.
6_data_booklet.pattern: C=O 1700-1750 covers aldehydes, ketones, acids and esters.
6_data_booklet.memorise: The statement that IR cannot give bond position is NOT printed; infer it.

7_elimination.short: Options A, B and C misdescribe what IR does.
7_elimination.why: Absorption causes bond vibration rather than a structural reaction, and bonds involving H appear in the table.
7_elimination.avoid: Accepting A because hydrogen is a small atom.

definitely_wrong.rule: Section 20 lists O-H absorptions.
Molar mass comes from mass spectrometry.
IR makes bonds vibrate; it does not chemically alter structure.

walkthrough.answer: D. It identifies bonds but not their position.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.9 IR bond identification; S3.2.12 combined data.
1_context.textbook_gap: Exams ask about limits, which require comparing techniques.

trap_boundaries: Molar mass comes from mass spectrometry, not IR.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Correct limit is about position; tempting answers misuse another technique.

3_novel_application.heuristic: Match each option to what its technique actually measures.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark for one letter.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not explain the absorption mechanism.

6_data_booklet.hack: Use the shared C=O row as a reminder that IR shows bond type, not exact location.

rules: Molar-mass statements belong to MS.
Hydrogen-containing bonds are detected in IR.

evidence.note: Answer D.
Correct limitation: identifies bonds, not their position.

cards.difficulty_signal: No percentage reported; bond identification is usually well prepared, so this is a lower-priority check.

cards.title: Alcohol class: only primary alcohols give acids

walkthrough.question:
Which compound can be oxidized by acidified potassium dichromate to an acid?
A. CH3CH(OH)CH3
B. CH3COCH3
C. CH3CH2CH(CH2OH)CH2CH3
D. CH3C(CH3)(OH)CH3
walkthrough.key_idea: A primary alcohol, with CH2OH, oxidizes to a carboxylic acid.
walkthrough.careful: A bracketed CH2OH branch still counts as primary.
procedure: Find the carbon bonded to OH.
Count the carbons attached to that carbon.
One: primary; two: secondary; three: tertiary.
Primary gives acid, secondary ketone, tertiary no oxidation.
tricks: Look for CH2OH anywhere, including inside brackets.
CH(OH) in a chain suggests secondary; C(R)(OH) with no H suggests tertiary.
if_lost: Which options actually contain an OH group?
How many carbons are attached to each OH-bearing carbon?
Which alcohol class can form a carboxylic acid?

1_context.short: Classify alcohols from condensed formulas, then predict the product.
1_context.why: The product depends on how many carbons are attached to the OH-bearing carbon, not on molecular size.
1_context.avoid: Choosing the longest molecule because it looks more complex.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.6: primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols should be included among structural isomers.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books usually show simple alcohols. This hides a primary OH inside a bracket in a branched molecule.

2_markscheme_logic.short: The answer is the only option with a primary alcohol.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Only primary alcohols can reach the acid stage, so identifying CH2OH decides the question.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Treating any alcohol as oxidizable to an acid; 13N.2.HL.TZ0.8 highlights tertiary alcohol behaviour.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: A secondary alcohol stops at a ketone, and a tertiary alcohol is not oxidized.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Correct C has CH2OH. Tempting A has OH on a carbon with two carbon neighbours.

3_novel_application.short: A long branched formula hides a simple CH2OH group.
3_novel_application.why: Oxidation depends on the OH-bearing carbon, so the rest of a long chain can be ignored.
3_novel_application.avoid: Assuming a bracketed group must be a simple alkyl branch.
3_novel_application.disguise: The primary alcohol appears in a bracket mid-formula.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Search for CH2OH first, regardless of formula length.

4_command_terms.short: No command term: an MCQ stem needs one reactant.
4_command_terms.why: Only the correct compound scores, so product equations are not needed.
4_command_terms.demands: Identify the compound forming an acid.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Scan for CH2OH, confirm, and move on.
5_time_efficiency.why: Primary alcohols are recognisable from this group, so the correct option can be found almost immediately.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip the colour change and mechanism.

6_data_booklet.short: Alcohol oxidation rules are not in the sections provided.
6_data_booklet.why: The sections provided hold spectral data, not reaction outcomes by alcohol class.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking for oxidation outcomes in the IR or NMR tables.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Primary, secondary and tertiary oxidation outcomes are NOT in the sections provided.

7_elimination.short: Secondary, ketone and tertiary options cannot give the acid.
7_elimination.why: The OH-bearing carbon in A has only one H, B has no OH, and D has none on its OH carbon.
7_elimination.avoid: Forgetting that a ketone is not an alcohol at all.

definitely_wrong.rule: Secondary alcohol forms a ketone, not an acid.
A ketone has no alcohol group to oxidize.
A tertiary alcohol resists this oxidation.

walkthrough.answer: C. It contains a primary CH2OH group, which can oxidize to a carboxylic acid.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S3.2.6 primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols.
1_context.textbook_gap: Exams hide the class inside brackets rather than presenting simple names.

trap_boundaries: Secondary alcohol stops at ketone; tertiary is not oxidized by this reagent.
Older reports note that acidified must be stated when reagents are asked for (08M.2.HL.TZ0.4).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Correct class identification decides the option.

3_novel_application.heuristic: Look at the OH carbon only.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark for one letter.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No equations required.

6_data_booklet.hack: No reaction rule in the sections provided.

rules: Ketones have no OH to oxidize.
Tertiary alcohols do not oxidize under these conditions.

evidence.note: Answer C.
Just over 62% identified the compound oxidized to a carboxylic acid.
Many recognised a tertiary alcohol would not undergo oxidation.
Acidified was often missing when dichromate was named.
